title: google/magika — Fast and accurate AI powered file content types detection
content:
Magika is a novel AI-powered file type detection tool that relies on the recent advance of deep learning to provide accurate detection. Under the hood, Magika employs a custom, highly optimized model that only weighs about a few MBs, and enables precise file identification within milliseconds, even when running on a single CPU. Magika has been trained and evaluated on a dataset of ~100M samples across 200+ content types (covering both binary and textual file formats), and it achieves an average ~99% accuracy on our test set.
Here is an example of what Magika command line output looks like:
Magika is used at scale to help improve Google users' safety by routing Gmail, Drive, and Safe Browsing files to the proper security and content policy scanners, processing hundreds billions samples on a weekly basis. Magika has also been integrated with VirusTotal (example) and abuse.ch (example).
For more context you can read our initial announcement post on Google's OSS blog, you can consult Magika's website, and you can read more in our research paper, published at the IEEE/ACM International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE) 2025.
You can try Magika without installing anything by using our web demo, which runs locally in your browser!
- Available as a command line tool written in Rust, a Python API, and additional bindings for Rust, JavaScript/TypeScript (with an experimental npm package, which powers our web demo), and GoLang (WIP).
- Trained and evaluated on a dataset of ~100M files across 200+ content types.
- On our test set, Magika achieves ~99% average precision and recall, outperforming existing approaches -- especially on textual content types.
- After the model is loaded (which is a one-off overhead), the inference time is about 5ms per file, even when run on a single CPU.
- You can invoke Magika with even thousands of files at the same time. You can also use -r for recursively scanning a directory.
- Near-constant inference time, independently from the file size; Magika only uses a limited subset of the file's content.
- Magika uses a per-content-type threshold system that determines whether to "trust" the prediction for the model, or whether to return a generic label, such as "Generic text document" or "Unknown binary data".
- The tolerance to errors can be controlled via different prediction modes, such as high-confidence ,medium-confidence , andbest-guess .
- The client and the bindings are already open source, and more is coming soon!
Magika ships a CLI written in Rust, and can be installed in several ways.
Via magika python package:
pipx install magika
Via brew (macOS / Linux)
brew install magika
Via installer script:
curl -LsSf https://securityresearch.google/magika/install.sh | sh
or:
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -c "irm https://securityresearch.google/magika/install.ps1 | iex"
Via magika-cli Rust package:
cargo install --locked magika-clipip install magikanpm install magika
Here you can find a number of quick examples just to get you started.
To learn about Magika's inner workings, see the Core Concepts section of Magika's website.

report.summary: Google's open-source Magika uses a tiny deep-learning model to identify file content types in milliseconds with ~99% accuracy, already scanning billions of files weekly for Gmail, Drive and Safe Browsing.
report.background: File type detection has long relied on signature-based tools like libmagic (the Unix 'file' command), which match magic bytes and heuristics. These are fast and dependency-free but brittle: they struggle with text-based formats, scripts, and files with misleading extensions, and they break down at the scale and diversity of modern cloud data. Magika was built inside Google to solve exactly that problem for security routing — deciding which policy and malware scanners should inspect an uploaded file. It replaces hand-written rules with a compact neural network trained on roughly 100 million samples spanning 200+ binary and textual content types. The work was published at ICSE 2025, is integrated with VirusTotal and abuse.ch, and is released under Apache 2.0 as a community project rather than an officially supported Google product.
key_points: Tiny model, millisecond inference: the shipped model weighs only a few megabytes and classifies a file in about 5ms on a single CPU. Inference time is near-constant regardless of file size because Magika only reads a limited subset of the file's content, making it practical for bulk and streaming workloads.

High accuracy across many formats: trained and evaluated on ~100M samples covering 200+ content types, it reaches roughly 99% average precision and recall on the test set, outperforming existing approaches, with the biggest gains on textual content types where signature tools are weakest.

Configurable confidence: a per-content-type threshold system decides whether to trust the model or fall back to generic labels like 'Generic text document' or 'Unknown binary data'. Users can pick high-confidence, medium-confidence or best-guess modes to trade recall against false positives.

Broad language support and easy install: it ships as a Rust CLI plus Python, JavaScript/TypeScript (npm) and in-progress Go bindings, installable via pipx, Homebrew, cargo, npm or one-line installer scripts. A browser web demo runs the model locally with no upload.

Proven at production scale: Google uses Magika to route Gmail, Drive and Safe Browsing files to appropriate security and content scanners, handling hundreds of billions of samples weekly. It is also integrated into VirusTotal and abuse.ch workflows.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Magika is a strong data point that small, task-specific models can beat decades of hand-tuned heuristics — and run at the edge for almost nothing. It reinforces the shift toward compact, purpose-built models over ever-larger general ones. For developers, it offers a drop-in upgrade over libmagic and python-magic in upload pipelines, MIME detection, log parsing, malware triage and data ingestion, with JSON output and recursive scanning built in. For regular users, it means safer, faster scanning of email attachments and cloud files with fewer misclassified documents. Caveats remain: the project is explicitly not an official Google product, and adversarial or truncated files can still fool any content-based classifier, so security-critical systems should pair it with other tools.
report.tools: Compare against libmagic/'file', python-magic, Apache Tika, filetype.py and fleep to see where Magika's deep-learning approach wins on text formats. Install Magika via pipx install magika, brew install magika, cargo install magika-cli or npm install magika, and try the browser demo. Also worth following: Magika's ICSE 2025 paper, the Google OSS blog announcement, and the VirusTotal and abuse.ch integrations for real-world use cases.
